dataset_used: TIMSS
performance_metrics: Not reported
standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Literature synthesis outcome (not student-level prediction), finding that This paper proposes a theoretical framework for constructing a mathematical cognitive model intended for cognitive diagnostic assessment and adaptive learning systems. Using TIMSS’s cognitive framework as a starting point, the authors list 16 cognitive attributes (S1–S16) and apply interpretive structural modeling (ISM) to derive hierarchical relationships among attributes via expert judgments. Specifically, 52 experts completed a “cognitive attribute relationship” questionnaire, which was converted into a structural self-interaction matrix (SSIM) using a 50% threshold (more than 25 experts indicating a relationship), followed by adjacency and reachability matrix construction in MATLAB. The preliminary five-level model is then revised using interviews/discussion with six mathematics education professors and validated through verbal reports from one randomly selected fourth-grade student on two TIMSS item types. No predictive performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/RMSE) are reported because the study’s contribution is model construction and conceptual validation rather than ML-based prediction. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

The authors mapped TALIS 2018 questionnaire scales onto an eight-dimension Leadership for Learning framework and used 12 leadership scale factor scores (six principal, six teacher) as indicators; one principal scale (instructional autonomy) was derived for the study. Limitations include that Google Trends measures relative search interest, not who searches or what stakeholders access, and that Google’s market share varies across countries (notably lower in China). The review reports mixed and context-dependent associations: some ICT contexts show positive relationships (notably perceived autonomy and, in many studies, ICT interest/competence), while other contexts show negative or null relationships depending on subject and country. The review emphasizes that the ICT–achievement relationship varies by ICT type (use vs availability vs interest vs autonomy vs social inclusion) and by country context, and it notes that all included studies are correlational and cross-sectional, limiting causal interpretation. Methodologically, the included studies use a range of approaches (e.g., multiple linear regression, HLM, SEM, logistic regression, propensity score matching, instrumental variables), but the review does not re-estimate effects or harmonize weighting/PV handling across studies. The main practical takeaway is that “moderate” ICT use and autonomy-oriented ICT engagement may be more beneficial than very low or very high use, though the evidence base remains heterogeneous. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

dataset_used: PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) Science domain (context questionnaires)
top_predictors: Inquiry-based learning (IBTEACH; WLE), Science interest (INTBRSCI; WLE), Teacher support (TEACHSUP; WLE), Disciplinary climate (DISCLISCI; WLE), Gender
performance_metrics: Mediation (PROCESS Model 4, 5,000 bootstraps): total effect B=0.194 (p<.001), direct effect B=0.155 (p<.001), indirect effect B=0.039 (20.1% of total; 95% CI above 0). Moderated mediation (PROCESS Model 59, 5,000 bootstraps): interaction IBTEACH×TEACHSUP predicting science self-efficacy B=0.049 (p<.001); interaction INTBRSCI×TEACHSUP predicting science self-efficacy B=-0.015 (p<.001). Model fit: R2=0.111 for the science self-efficacy outcome model (standardized). Effect size: Cohen’s f2 for final model = 0.125 (small).
standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) science context questionnaire the study leveraged inquiry-based learning (IBTEACH), science interest (INTBRSCI), and teacher support (TEACHSUP), controlling for disciplinary climate and gender, to model science self-efficacy (SCIEEFF; WLE). It found that inquiry-based learning had a significant positive direct association with science self-efficacy (B=0.155), and that science interest partially mediated this relationship with an indirect effect accounting for 20.1% of the total effect (indirect B=0.039). Teacher support strengthened the direct effect of inquiry-based learning on science self-efficacy (interaction B=0.049) while weakening the indirect pathway through science interest (interaction B=-0.015), indicating a mediating–moderating pattern. This indicates that improving inquiry-based science instruction should be paired with strategies that sustain students’ science interest while leveraging teacher support to maximize self-efficacy gains, though the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.

standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 CBMA U.S. the study leveraged item-level action and score variability measures (average actions, unique actions, predominant-action proportion, and predominant-score proportion) to explain differences in item-level predictive accuracy. It found that items with very limited behavioral diversity (e.g., only two unique actions) provide insufficient signal for learning, while having more than two unique actions supports above-chance prediction; other variability measures showed weaker or no clear monotonic relationships. This indicates that assessment designers should include interactive, multi-step behaviors that generate diverse action traces to enable reliable process-data-based competency prediction, especially when sample sizes are limited.

dataset_used: TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Science (44 countries) — science achievement (Plausible Values BSSSCI01–BSSSCI05)
target_variable: Curriculum effect on science achievement (Average Treatment Effect via propensity score matching)
top_predictors: Curriculum type (integrated vs separated) (ITCOURSE), Socio-economic background (BSBGHER), Like to learn science (BSBGSLS), Confidence about science (BSBGSCS), Instructional clarity (BSBGICS)
performance_metrics: Propensity score estimation via stacked ensemble (base learners: k-NN, Random Forest, Naive Bayes; meta-learner: logistic regression) with KNN matching. Propensity score prediction accuracy on test set: 0.9998. After matching, Mann–Whitney U tests with Bonferroni correction show integrated curricula have significantly higher science achievement than separated curricula for each PV (Cohen’s d around 0.2; e.g., PV1 d=0.22 with integrated mean 546.62 vs separated mean 515.68; PV2 d=0.20; PV3 d=0.24; PV4 d=0.23; PV5 d=0.20).
standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Science the study leveraged propensity score matching based on socio-economic background, student attitudes, and instructional clarity to estimate the average treatment effect of integrated versus separated science curricula on science achievement plausible values, finding that integrated curricula produced a statistically significant but small advantage (Cohen’s d ≈0.2 across PVs). This indicates that integrated curricula may be beneficial in practice, but the magnitude is modest, so education systems should treat curriculum integration as one component within a broader package that ensures instructional prerequisites and high-quality implementation, while recognizing that matching on observed covariates cannot fully eliminate unobserved confounding.

dataset_used: Simulation study of IRT-latent regression with PVs (N=1000 test takers; 40 items; 2PL/3PL; PVs M=20)
target_variable: Population mean and distribution moments of latent proficiency (PV-based estimators)
top_predictors: Number of predictors (P), Items per test taker (J), Item missingness condition, IRT item model (2PL/3PL), Focal group membership
performance_metrics: Bias patterns reported in Tables 1 and 3–6: as P increases, bias for population mean/skewness becomes increasingly negative in difficult 3PL; variance and kurtosis bias increases; extreme percentiles (10th/90th) show stronger outward bias than median. Example magnitude: in difficult 3PL with Missing and J=4, mean population variance estimate exceeds true variance by 52.7%; in moderate 2PL with No missing and J=4, variance overestimation is 2.4%.
standardized_conclusion: Using simulation data for IRT-latent regression with PVs, the study leveraged number of predictors (P), items per test taker (J), item missingness condition, and IRT item model type to estimate population moments and percentiles of latent proficiency, finding that estimator bias grows with P particularly when measurement precision is low for a substantial share of test takers (e.g., difficult 3PL and Missing). This indicates that expanding the predictor set in large-scale assessments can undermine validity unless assessment designs ensure at least moderate measurement precision for all test takers, especially for low-proficiency groups.

performance_metrics: Appendix C/D and Tables 7–11: plug-in and PV-based estimators are approximately equivalent for means and variances when PVs are generated conditional on fixed maximum-likelihood regression parameters; however, PV-based variance estimators using the operational procedure (PVs generated conditional on sampled regression parameters) produce additional positive bias relative to plug-in variance estimators, increasing with P.
standardized_conclusion: Using simulation data for IRT-latent regression with PVs, the study leveraged number of predictors (P) and assessment design conditions (J and missingness) to compare PV-based and plug-in variance estimation, finding that PV-based variance estimates become more positively biased when PVs are generated conditional on sampled regression parameters rather than fixed ML estimates. performance_metrics: Not reported
standardized_conclusion: Using PISA the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict problem-solving, finding that This scoping review used structural topic modeling (STM) to identify recurring themes in 221 empirical studies that used process/log data in large-scale assessments. The review’s “inputs” were the abstracts of included papers (with citations/section headings removed and standard NLP preprocessing such as lowercasing, stopword removal, and stemming), and the “outputs” were topic assignments based on the highest posterior topic probability. The authors estimated STM models with 5–10 topics and selected a six-topic solution using semantic coherence and FREX, then manually coded subtopics and extracted theories/methods from full papers. The six recurring topics were response time models, response time-general, aberrant test-taking behavior, action sequences, complex problem-solving, and digital writing. The study does not report predictive performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/RMSE) because it is not training ML models on student outcomes; instead, it maps how process data are used and which theories are invoked, with limitations related to topic-model assignment ambiguity and the exclusion of papers without abstracts. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

dataset_used: PISA 2015 (Norway) Grade 9/10 Science — Task 2 (modified Running in Hot Weather field-trial item)
target_variable: Inquiry performance latent profiles (strategic vs emergent vs disengaged) from process-log indicators
top_predictors: Interactive strategy (multivariable), Number of actions, Number of trials, Time before first action, Time-on-task
performance_metrics: Latent profile analysis: three-profile solution with significant VLMR and LMR-LRT tests; high entropy and distinct class separation/homogeneity (exact values not reported). Descriptive profile means: Strategic Maction=14.99, Mtrial=4.58, Mtime-before-first-action=31.69s, Mtime-on-task=186.58s; Emergent Mtime-on-task=102.59s; Disengaged Mtime-on-task=43.97s. Transfer to multivariable VOTAT: 38.7% showed high probability of adapting VOTAT into multivariable context. Additional analysis (Association between inquiry-teaching practices and inquiry performance profiles (MANOVA profile mean differences)): MANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc comparisons (Table 3): Debate differentiated all three profiles (F=17.53, p<.01; pairwise: 1>3, 1>2, 2>3). Several items showed strategic>disengaged and/or emergent>disengaged differences: Lab (F=5.18, p<.01; 1>3), Draw (F=9.42, p<.01; 1>3, 2>3), Idea (F=5.56, p<.01; 1>3), Design (F=4.72, p<.01; 1>3), Test (F=3.17, p<.01; 1>3). No significant differences for Explain, Argue, and Concept across profiles (per text).
standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 (Norway) Grade 9/10 Science data for Task 2, the study leveraged interactive strategy use and log-derived exploration and timing indicators to identify three latent inquiry-performance profiles, finding that the strategic profile showed the highest likelihood of using the interactive strategy and the highest time-on-task and exploration, while emergent students took longer but still had low probabilities of explaining claim–evidence relationships. This indicates that classroom support should target both multivariable coordination and the explicit claim–evidence linking process, not merely increasing exploration time or strategy attempts.

standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Literature synthesis outcome (not student-level prediction), finding that This article is a methodological contribution that argues for a design-based perspective in official reporting of international large-scale assessment (LSA) results, while clarifying how model-based components (IRT measurement models and latent background models) are used to generate plausible values. It discusses five analytical choices that can change the meaning of proficiency estimates: (1) the functional form of item response functions (e.g., 1PL vs 2PL vs 3PL/4PL), (2) handling local dependence and multidimensionality (e.g., testlets), (3) whether and how test-taking behavior (omission, speed, response times) is modeled, (4) treatment of country differential item functioning (DIF) and partial invariance for cross-country comparisons, and (5) approaches to trend estimation (original vs marginal trends; linking errors). The paper emphasizes that model misspecification can affect reliability and uncertainty, and that resampling-based standard error estimation can support design-based inference even under misspecified likelihoods. It also highlights fairness/validity concerns when scoring rules depend on test-taking behavior or when DIF handling effectively changes the set of items contributing to comparisons. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.
